seoTitle: How to Connect GitHub to Power BI for Repo Tracking
metaDescription: Install Power BI's official GitHub template app from AppSource, or build a custom Web connection with a personal access token when you need Enterprise support or data the template doesn't cover.
intro:
Power BI still has no GitHub button inside Get Data, but Microsoft does publish an official GitHub template app through AppSource that a lot of guides skip past. Point it at a repository and it builds a ready-made dashboard covering contributor activity, issue timing, and pull request counts, with almost no report-building required.

This guide installs that app first, then covers the custom Web-connector route for anyone who needs GitHub Enterprise support or data the template doesn't expose. Both paths authenticate with a GitHub personal access token instead of an OAuth prompt inside Power BI.

steps.heading: Start from your Power BI workspace
steps.body: Everything begins in My workspace, the default landing page in the Power BI service. Reports, semantic models, and dashboards are listed here by name, type, owner, and last refresh time. This is also where the GitHub-fed report will live once it's built, alongside anything else your workspace already has.

image.caption: The Power BI service's My workspace view, listing existing reports, semantic models, and dashboards by name, type, and owner.

steps.heading: Install the official GitHub template app
steps.body:
Open Apps from the workspace's left navigation. This opens Power BI's AppSource marketplace, not a custom-connector picker, and Microsoft lists a GitHub template app there under that exact name. Search for it, click Get it now, then Install.

Power BI creates a new workspace holding a ready-made dashboard, report, and semantic model: commit activity by contributor, issue open-and-close times, and pull request counts, once you connect it to your own data. The template doesn't support GitHub Enterprise Server or Enterprise Cloud. If that's what your repos run on, skip ahead to the custom Web-connector steps.

image.caption: Power BI's Apps marketplace, where the official GitHub template app is listed by name alongside other Microsoft and third-party apps.

steps.heading: Generate a GitHub personal access token
steps.body:
On github.com, go to Settings, then Developer settings, then Personal access tokens. GitHub recommends fine-grained tokens over the classic kind: you can scope one to a single repository with Contents set to Read-only, while a classic token's repo scope reaches every repository you can already access, personal and organizational alike.

For a repository owned by an organization, that org may need to approve a fine-grained token before it can read anything inside it. A classic token skips that approval step but keeps the wider reach. Paste whichever type you choose into the template app's Connect your data screen when it asks for authentication.

steps.heading: Build a custom connection when the template isn't enough
steps.body: The template app covers one repository's contributors, issues, and pull requests. For GitHub Enterprise, several repositories combined, or a metric the template doesn't expose, build the connection yourself instead. In Power BI Desktop, use Get Data, choose Web, and point it at the GitHub REST API endpoint for the data you want. Paste your token into the HTTP request header, not the URL, so it isn't stored in a saved query or a shared file.

steps.heading: Shape the JSON and build your visuals
steps.body: GitHub's API returns nested JSON. Power Query needs a handful of Expand and Convert to Table steps to pull commit author, date, and message into their own columns. Filter out bot commits and merge commits if they'd skew a contributor activity chart. From there, build what the template didn't already give you: a line chart of commits over time, or a table comparing repositories side by side.

steps.heading: Publish and schedule a refresh
steps.body: Publish the report to the workspace you started in, then set a scheduled refresh from the dataset's settings. GitHub's API applies rate limits per token, so an hourly refresh is plenty for most teams; anything tighter risks hitting those limits for no real benefit.

troubleshooting.problem: GitHub doesn't show up when searching Get Data
troubleshooting.cause: Power BI has no dedicated GitHub connector in Get Data. The only Microsoft-built options are the GitHub template app in AppSource and a hand-built Web connection to the REST API.
troubleshooting.fix: Install the template app from Apps, or use Get Data, then Web, against the GitHub REST API instead.

troubleshooting.problem: Connect your data returns nothing for an organization's repository
troubleshooting.cause: A fine-grained token needs the organization's approval before it can read an org-owned repo. Without it, the request comes back empty instead of showing an error.
troubleshooting.fix: Ask an org owner to approve the token under the organization's fine-grained token settings, or switch to a classic token with the repo scope.

troubleshooting.problem: The GitHub template app won't connect to your repositories at all
troubleshooting.cause: The template app doesn't support GitHub Enterprise Server or Enterprise Cloud.
troubleshooting.fix: Build a custom Web connection to your Enterprise instance's API endpoint instead of using the template app.

faq.question: Does Power BI have a built-in GitHub connector?
faq.answer: Not in Get Data. Microsoft instead publishes a GitHub template app through AppSource, and a custom Web connection to GitHub's REST API covers anything that template doesn't.

faq.question: Does the GitHub template app work with GitHub Enterprise?
faq.answer: No. It only supports github.com repositories. Enterprise Server and Enterprise Cloud need a custom Web connection instead.

faq.question: What GitHub token permissions do I need?
faq.answer: A fine-grained token with Contents set to Read, scoped to the repository you're pulling from, or a classic token with the repo scope if you'd rather skip organization approval and accept broader access.

faq.question: Can Power BI show data from more than one GitHub repository?
faq.answer: Yes, though the template app is built around one repository at a time. To combine several in one report, install it more than once into separate workspaces, or query multiple repos through a custom Web connection.

faq.question: Is a paid GitHub plan required for this?
faq.answer: No. Basic repository and commit data is available through the GitHub API on free accounts, provided you have read access and a valid token.

verifiedNote: Click path and screens for the workspace and Apps marketplace come from a walkthrough recorded in July 2025. Re-checked in September 2026: GitHub's own documentation on personal access token scopes and organization approval was fetched and read directly. The GitHub template app's feature set, its single-repository scope, and its lack of GitHub Enterprise support were corroborated through Microsoft's AppSource listings and Power BI community documentation, since Microsoft's specific Learn article for it redirected to a general index instead of loading directly in this session. This pass added the template-app path entirely; the original draft jumped straight to a hand-built Web connection despite an official pre-built option existing.
